summary:
Santa Catarina stands under Brazil's national framework, and its own record shows a state legislature moving against trans and LGBTIQ people while the courts have narrowed the state's own protections.

The state constitution carries an anti-discrimination clause dating to 2002 that lists sexual orientation among the protected grounds, but as of 2019 it does not address discrimination against transgender people. Two state statutes that did cover gender identity have been stripped back: State Law No. 12,534 of 4 April 2003 was repealed on 8 October 2015 by Complementary Law No. 656, and Complementary Law No. 527 of 28 December 2010, which penalised private entities and state servants for discriminatory acts on grounds of gender or sexual orientation with fines of R$2,500 rising to R$5,000 on repeat plus licence suspension or revocation, lost Articles 2 VI and VII when the Supreme Federal Court declared them unconstitutional in ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018.

Legislative activity in Santa Catarina has run against trans and LGBTIQ rights. From January 2019 to June 2025 state deputies introduced 19 anti-LGBTQIA+ bills against 4 pro-LGBTQIA+ bills, including proposals to bar minors from hormone therapy, surgical interventions and other gender-transition care and to prohibit neutral language in official communications; 4 of the anti bills were archived and none was enacted. As of 2025, 19 anti-LGBTQ bills had been tabled in the Legislative Assembly with 11 authored by the Liberal Party. In December 2023 the Assembly's Constitution and Justice Committee approved a bill prohibiting transgender women from participating in women's sports, still under review as of 18 August 2026. A 2026 count recorded 271 unconstitutional laws processed in the state since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, about 70% involving the trans and travesti community and 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court; a separate count covering January 2015 to October 2025 found at least 271 such acts across the Legislative Assembly and 295 municipal chambers, 41% attacking gender and sexuality with particular focus on LGBTIQ+ people, 36% already in force and only 11% judicially annulled, concentrated in the Vale do Itajaí and accelerating in the last five years.

Restroom and facilities access is contested. On 21 January 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed State Law No. 19,686/2026 requiring all public and private educational institutions from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms; the Federal University of Santa Catarina installed signs from 18 June 2026 indicating restrooms may be used in accordance with gender identity. In a 2014 Florianópolis shopping-mall case, a trans woman denied access to the women's restroom won R$15,000 in moral damages at first instance under the Consumer Defense Code, lost on appeal before the Court of Justice of Santa Catarina, and on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Court voted 8-3 to dismiss her appeal on procedural grounds that the claim had pleaded only consumer-law damages, issuing no binding constitutional ruling on trans bathroom access; an extraordinary appeal to the Inter-American Court of Human Rights against both courts followed in August 2025.

Education and school policy are also restricted. Gender-neutral language was banned in state schools by decree of Governor Carlos Moises on 15 June 2021 until overturned 6 May 2025 by the Supreme Federal Court, and banned in Joinville public office by law of 20 December 2021 until struck down 3 August 2022 by the Court of Justice. On 1 April 2026 Governor Jorginho Mello signed a law published 6 April allowing parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics; on 15 October 2025 the Supreme Federal Court struck down a 2015 Tubarão law that had prohibited teaching of gender and sexual orientation in schools.

Document and registry practice in the state runs through the courts rather than statute. Since 2020 people in Santa Catarina have obtained documents recording non-binary gender through the courts or notarial offices, although no specific state law prescribes this; in 2021 Idris Kawabe became the first person in Santa Catarina to judicially change documents to a neutral gender, and judicial actions remain necessary because no state law recognises the marker. The Army provides that a person in the draft cohort expressing a gender identity other than male who holds a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment is treated as non-binary in the same manner as intersex individuals and exempt from mandatory military service.

Marriage and relationship recognition are processed locally. On 29 April 2013 the Corregedoria-Geral da Justiça of Santa Catarina authorised notarial and civil-registry offices to process marriage habilitations regardless of the sex of the spouses, allowing same-sex couples where both partners reside in the state to formalise civil marriage and expanding Article 629 of the CGJ Code of Norms beyond the stable union recognised since 2011. A legal guide updated 5 April 2026 names Florianópolis among Brazil's broadly welcoming major cities, with active LGBTQ+ communities, pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages, adoptions and name or gender-marker changes, while smaller cities and rural areas may present more social friction.

Violence and hostility are documented in state figures. In 2024 three murders of trans people were recorded in Santa Catarina. The 2024 Brazilian Public Security Yearbook reported 85 cases of intentional bodily injury against LGBTQ individuals in the state, with low rates attributed to underreporting. On 3 September 2026 the Court of Justice ordered the parents of a gay teenager in Jaguaruna to pay R$100,000 in compensation after kicking him out and exposing his sexual orientation on social media. In Florianópolis, a judge of the 1st Civil Court, M. C. F. Ribeiro da Silva, blocked immigration authorities from deporting an Italian citizen who had lived over ten years in a stable relationship with a lesbian Brazilian.

Political hostility at the national level has produced a surge of anti-LGBTIQ proposals, including efforts to repeal marriage equality, though constitutional guarantees and federal criminal provisions adopted after the 2019 Supreme Federal Tribunal ruling continue to prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity. In September 2025 the federal government reinstated the National LGBTI+ Health Technical Committee, a participatory mechanism dissolved in 2019, for shaping and monitoring inclusive public-health policy.
tangentialFactors:
Santa Catarina's trajectory contrasts with the national framework in direction: federal courts have expanded trans recognition and criminalised transphobia on a par with racism, while the state's own statutes covering gender-identity discrimination have been repealed or struck down and its legislature has produced a sustained volume of restrictive bills. A 2026 count found 271 unconstitutional laws processed in the state since 2015 against women's or LGBTQ rights, roughly 70% involving the trans and travesti community, with 41% ruled unconstitutional by the Supreme Federal Court and only 11% judicially annulled, leaving a substantial share in force.

The restroom litigation shows the limits of the national protections in practice: the Supreme Federal Court's 6 June 2024 dismissal was procedural rather than a ruling on the merits, so no binding constitutional precedent on trans bathroom access exists, and the case remains before the Inter-American Court of Human Rights after an August 2025 extraordinary appeal.

State-level restrictions on school facilities and curriculum sit alongside a federal court ruling of 15 October 2025 striking down a municipal teaching ban, indicating that municipal and state measures in this area have been vulnerable to constitutional challenge even as newer state statutes are adopted.
localsOnly:
State Law No. 19,686/2026, signed 21 January 2026, binds all public and private educational institutions in Santa Catarina from preschool through higher and vocational education to maintain strictly separate male and female restrooms and changing rooms. The Federal University of Santa Catarina's contrary signage from 18 June 2026 reflects institutional policy rather than an exemption from the statute.

The law signed 1 April 2026 and published 6 April permitting parents to prohibit children from participating in classes on LGBTQ topics applies to schooling in the state. Gender-neutral language remains banned in Joinville public office after the Court of Justice struck down the 20 December 2021 law on 3 August 2022 only in part, and the state-school ban of 15 June 2021 was overturned on 6 May 2025.

Complementary Law No. 527's surviving provisions still penalise private legal entities and, where applicable, state public servants for promoting, permitting or tolerating discriminatory acts on grounds of gender or sexual orientation, with complaints routed to the State Secretariat of Public Security and Defense of the Citizen and fines paid into the State Civil Police Improvement Fund; Articles 2 VI and VII, struck down in ADI 5307 on 29 October 2018, are the provisions that no longer apply.

Non-binary gender markers in Santa Catarina are obtained through judicial or notarial action rather than administrative process, because no state statute provides for them; legal sex entry on birth certificates remains required. Military-service exemption on non-binary grounds depends on holding a final, unappealable court ruling or civil registry amendment.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether State Law No. 19,686/2026 has been challenged in court or is subject to any injunction; its status as of the record date is unsourced.

Whether the 2023 bill barring transgender women from women's sports has advanced beyond committee review after 18 August 2026 is not sourced, nor is the fate of the 1 April 2026 parental-opt-out law on challenge.

The 2026 count of 271 unconstitutional laws and the January 2015 to October 2025 count of 271 acts appear to describe overlapping or identical datasets from different publishers; the record does not reconcile them, and the share currently in force is stated only for the second count.

No figure in the inventory gives a denominator for the three trans killings recorded in Santa Catarina in 2024 or for the 85 intentional-bodily-injury cases in the 2024 yearbook, so neither can be compared to the state's general homicide or assault rate; the yearbook's own attribution of low counts to underreporting leaves the true magnitude unknown.

The record does not document any Santa Catarina-specific incident of trans-specific violence after 2024, and does not document state-level enforcement practice under the surviving provisions of Complementary Law No. 527.
